subject: Hasarius adansoni jumping spider
structure_mechanism: four-tier principal-eye retina plus lens chromatic aberration; green-sensitive receptor layers receive different amounts of defocus
claim: Jumping spiders can extract distance from image defocus in a single principal eye: wavelength-dependent chromatic aberration changes blur in a predictable way, and behavioral jump distance shifts accordingly. This is a distinct depth channel from binocular stereopsis or motion parallax.
limitations: The strongest behavioral demonstration is in H. adansoni; the mechanism should not be generalized to all spiders or treated as the only possible depth cue in all salticids.
contradictions: Popular summaries saying jumping spiders simply have 'super-sharp eight-eye vision' miss that deliberate optical defocus in one retinal tier carries useful range information.

sources.title: Depth Perception from Image Defocus in a Jumping Spider
sources.authors: Takashi Nagata; Mitsumasa Koyanagi; Hisao Tsukamoto; Motohiro Saeki; Katsushi Isono; Yoshinori Shichida; Fumio Tokunaga; Michiyo Kinoshita; Kentaro Arikawa; Akihisa Terakita

subject: Thermonectus marmoratus larval visual system
structure_mechanism: multiple camera-type larval eyes with layered retinas and bifocal lenses; principal eyes E1 and E2 specialize for different working distances
claim: The larval diving beetle partitions near and far vision across two principal eyes: both E1 and E2 have bifocal optics, E1 is better suited to far vision and E2 to near vision, while focused-image positions shift across retinal layers over the hunting range. The geometry could support unilateral range finding.
function: underwater prey detection, range estimation and visually guided striking
limitations: Optical/anatomical organization is strongly demonstrated, but the exact neural computation converting layer-specific focus into distance remains inferential; 'unilateral range finding' is supported behaviorally but the specific layered-retina mechanism is not fully reconstructed.
contradictions: Calling these merely 'simple insect larval eyes' is misleading: they are single-chamber camera-type eyes with unusually elaborate bifocal and multi-retinal organization.

sources.title: Multitasking in an eye: the unusual organization of the Thermonectus marmoratus principal larval eyes allows for far and near vision and might aid in depth perception

subject: African dung beetle celestial cue reweighting
species_group: diurnal and nocturnal ball-rolling dung beetles
structure_mechanism: polarization-sensitive dorsal eye input integrated with celestial-body azimuth signals by central-complex compass neurons
claim: Nocturnal dung beetles dynamically reweight celestial channels with ambient intensity: at daylight levels a celestial body dominates, but at full-moon-like intensity polarization becomes the dominant compass cue; homologous central-complex neurons switch their tuning in the same direction. Closely related diurnal beetles instead retain celestial-body dominance across tested light levels.
function: straight-line escape/navigation away from dung competition under radically different illumination regimes
limitations: The study establishes behavioral and neural cue weighting in the tested African species and conditions; it does not imply that all dung beetles or all nocturnal insects use the same hierarchy.
contradictions: The common shorthand 'dung beetles navigate by polarized light' is incomplete: cue priority is species- and illumination-dependent, and nocturnal animals can switch the neural weighting of celestial cues.

sources.title: Neural coding underlying the cue preference for celestial orientation
sources.authors: Basil el Jundi; Eric J Warrant; Marcus J Byrne; Lana Khaldy; Emily Baird; Jochen Smolka; Marie Dacke
